title: Listening to Wildfires: Low-Frequency Rumbles Could Revolutionize Fire Tracking
summary:
Most fire spotters use their eyes, but researchers have shown that ears can work too—especially for sounds too low for humans to hear. In a new study published in Geophysical Research Letters, scientists deployed acoustic sensors near a prescribed burn in Idaho. These sensors picked up infrasound, frequencies below 20 hertz, which humans can't perceive. By tracking this low rumble, they mapped the fire's spread over several hours.

This is significant because wildfires in their early stages are often hard to spot—they're low to the ground and far from towns. Satellites and aircraft require direct line of sight, which clouds and trees can block. Infrasound, however, can travel through such obstacles, providing "very fast alerts about how a fire is changing," says Jake Anderson, a geophysicist at Boise State University who led the study.

The team placed over 90 sensors in eight arrays across southwestern Idaho. Each sensor weighed less than a kilogram and was about the size of a paperback book. The largest array, nearly 2 kilometers from the fire, accurately tracked the flames. The rumble persisted even after the helicopter that ignited the fire left, confirming the fire itself was the source.

This isn't the first time infrasound has detected fires—last year, another group mapped a hotter fire in Florida. But this Idaho fire was in a damp landscape, so it burned less intensely, showing the technique works for weaker fires too.

However, there are challenges. Wind produces lots of infrasound, which could interfere. As Cody Evers, an environmental scientist at Portland State University, warns, "Lots of wind around these sensors could create all sorts of problems."

Still, the potential is exciting. If this technology can be refined, it could give firefighters an early-warning system that works even in poor visibility, potentially saving lives and property.
why_it_matters: As climate change makes wildfires larger and harder to control, every extra minute of early warning gives communities more time to evacuate — and teenagers growing up in fire-prone regions will be the people living with, and improving, these detection systems.

background_read: Infrasound is an old tool being used in a new way: for decades, the global monitoring network of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty Organization has listened for ultra-low sound waves from nuclear explosions.
Seismologists also track giant volcanic eruptions through infrasound — the huge eruption of Krakatoa in Indonesia in the late nineteenth century sent pressure waves circling the globe several times.
Wildfire infrasound is created when heat makes air churn violently, and those pressure waves can travel hundreds of kilometers without being blocked by clouds, trees, or mountains.

Boise State University, where study leader Jake Anderson works, is a public research university in Idaho that studies Earth science and wildfire behavior, and Geophysical Research Letters is a fast-turnaround peer-reviewed journal for Earth and space science.

Still, the technique has limits: Cody Evers, an environmental scientist at Portland State University (a public university in Oregon), warns that windy conditions create infrasound noise, which is why the milder Idaho burn — compared with last year's hotter Florida fire — was a useful test of how well the method works on weak fires.

perspectives.description: They would gain an early-warning tool that works when smoke, clouds, or darkness hide the flames. Faster alerts about a fire's changing behavior could help them decide where to send crews before a small fire becomes a disaster.

They worry that wind-generated infrasound could trigger false alarms or hide a real fire's signal. The study is promising, they say, but one damp Idaho burn does not prove the method works in every landscape and weather condition.

They see this as a natural extension of technology already used for nuclear test monitoring and volcano studies. For them, the value is in proving that weak, low-temperature fires produce measurable infrasound — a new piece of physical knowledge.

They imagine combining infrasound arrays with satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to filter out wind noise. If that works, remote forests could be monitored continuously for a fraction of the cost of manned aircraft patrols.
